title: What a Cloud ERP Implementation Actually Looks Like for Mid-Market Businesses
snippet: A cloud ERP implementation moves through seven phases, from data migration and parallel running to go-live and optimisation. This guide explains what each involves for mid-market finance teams. The post What a Cloud ERP Implementation Actually Looks Like for Mid-Market Businesses appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
A cloud ERP implementation is the structured project of moving a business’s finance and operational processes onto a new cloud system: migrating data, configuring the system to match how the business works, connecting it to other tools, training people, running old and new side by side, and going live. For a mid-market business, it is less a software installation than a change programme that happens to involve software. 

That distinction matters because an implementation touches month-end, relies on a finance team that is already busy, and affects every process that uses financial data. This guide sets out what the work involves, phase by phase, for FDs, financial controllers and project sponsors building a business case. If you are still deciding whether a change is needed, start with is your finance system holding back business growth? This article picks up once the decision is made. 

Key takeaways

Implementation is a phased process, not one project. Data migration, configuration, integration, user adoption, parallel running, go-live and optimisation each carry different owners and risks. 

Data and people need as much planning as technology. Data clean-up and user adoption are phases that benefit from early, deliberate attention. 

Duration depends on your business. Entity count, number of integrations, data quality and finance team availability set the timeline, not the software alone. 

Internal time is the hidden cost. Plan for named finance team members to be released from day-to-day work throughout. 

Parallel running builds confidence. Running old and new together shows whether the numbers agree before the business relies on them. 

Here’s what we cover:

Every implementation is different, but the sequence is consistent. The table summarises what happens in each phase, what is asked of the finance team and where projects most often go wrong.

Phase 

What happens 

Finance team involvement 

Common pitfall 

Data migration 

Data is cleaned, mapped and loaded into the new system. 

Decide how much history to bring across; sign off mapping. 

Migrating poor-quality data unchanged. 

Configuration 

The system is set up for entities, chart of accounts, approvals and reporting. 

Define requirements and make design decisions quickly. 

Rebuilding old workarounds instead of redesigning the process. 

Integration 

The system is connected to banks, payroll, CRM and other tools. 

Document every data feed and its owner. 

Hidden dependencies discovered late. 

User adoption 

People are trained on new processes and roles. 

Name champions; protect training time. 

One training session before go-live. 

Parallel running 

Old and new systems run side by side for at least one close. 

Reconcile outputs and explain every difference. 

Cutting it short under deadline pressure. 

Go-live 

The new system becomes the system of record. 

Run the cutover checklist; stay close to the project team. 

Going live at a peak period with no agreed pause criteria. 

Optimisation 

Reports, workflows and controls are refined after live use. 

Review what is not working; own the deferred list. 

Treating go-live as the end of the project. 

The seven phases in more detail

1. Data migration

Data migration moves what the new system needs from the old one: the chart of accounts, open balances, open invoices, supplier and customer records and, usually, some period of history. The finance team decides what comes across and the implementation partner builds and tests the loads. A common problem is moving data unchanged, so duplicate suppliers, inactive accounts and inconsistent coding follow it into the new system. Agree early how much history is genuinely needed, clean master data before loading, and expect several trial migrations rather than one. Reconciling migrated balances back to the old ledger at each stage is the safeguard, and our guide to account reconciliation covers the discipline involved. 

2. Configuration

Configuration shapes the system around how the business works: entity structure, chart of accounts, approval rules, tax settings, reporting dimensions and user roles. It is where finance leaders spend most of their decision time, and where slow decisions create the most delay. The pitfall is rebuilding the old process exactly as it was, including the workarounds the new system was meant to remove. Document current processes honestly, decide what should change, and nominate one person with the authority to settle design questions. For groups, entity structure decisions made now determine how easily the business can add entities later, a theme covered in multi-entity finance: acquire and expand.

3. Integration

Integration connects the finance system to the rest of the business: banks, payroll, expenses, CRM, billing, procurement and any specialist tools. Finance owns the requirement, the vendor or IT builds the connection, and the people who run the other system must be involved. The pitfall is the dependency nobody listed, usually a spreadsheet or manual file transfer that quietly feeds a report. Build a complete inventory of every data feed in and out of the current system, with an owner for each. Processes such as AP automation depend on clean connections to purchasing and banking, so test these flows end to end, not just individually. 

4. User adoption

User adoption is the phase that determines whether the new system is used as designed. It covers training, role changes, new approval habits and the dip in confidence that follows any change in daily tools. Involve the people who do the work early, name a champion in each team and schedule training close to go-live, with refreshers afterwards. A single session before launch is the common pitfall: it is forgotten by the second week. Expect questions and workarounds to appear after launch, and make them easy to raise.

5. Parallel running

Parallel running means operating the old and new systems side by side, often for a full period close, depending on the agreed implementation and testing approach. It is where the finance team builds confidence in the new numbers and finds migration or configuration errors while the old system is still the system of record. Every difference should be explained, not averaged away. It is also the phase that most increases workload, because the team is effectively closing twice, and it is often cut when timetables tighten. Plan cover for that in advance.

6. Go-live

Go-live is the cutover: the new system becomes the system of record and the old one becomes read-only. It is usually less dramatic than people expect when earlier phases have gone well. The finance team runs the agreed cutover checklist, confirms opening balances and stays in close contact with the project team through the first days and first close. Timing matters: avoiding year-end, audit fieldwork and peak trading periods reduces risk. Agree beforehand who can pause the cutover, and under what conditions. 

7. Post-implementation optimisation

Go-live is the start of the benefit, not the end of the project. In the following months, teams refine reports, simplify workflows, tighten controls and add the improvements deferred to keep the first release manageable. The pitfall is declaring the project finished at go-live and leaving users to solve problems alone. Plan a review after the first full close and another after the first quarter, with a list of deferred items and an owner for each. Faster closes are a common aim, but they may not arrive in the first month; see why UK finance teams can’t close faster for what drives the time in a close. 

How long does a cloud ERP implementation take?

There is no honest single answer. Duration depends on the number of entities, how many integrations are needed, the quality of existing data, how much the business wants to change its processes, and how much time the finance team can give the project alongside its day job. A single-entity business with clean data and few integrations looks very different from a multi-entity group with legacy tools to connect. Ask any vendor for a plan built on your own scope, with the assumptions behind it stated, rather than a headline figure.

What to budget in internal time, and what to ask a vendor

The implementation partner delivers much of the technical work, but the business supplies decisions, data knowledge and testing. Budget for named finance team members to be released for a meaningful share of their time during configuration, migration testing and parallel running, and for a project sponsor with the authority to resolve disagreements between departments. Before choosing a partner, ask: 

Question to ask 

Why it matters 

Who will be on our project team, and will they stay on it? 

Continuity of people matters more than the plan on paper. 

What do you assume we will provide, and how much of our time does that need? 

Surfaces the internal commitment before the business case is signed off. 

How do you approach data migration and testing? 

Reveals how many trial loads happen and who signs them off. 

What happens when scope changes? 

Shows how change control is handled. 

What support is there after go-live? 

Confirms optimisation is planned, not optional.

Planning implementation into your business case

In a business case, implementation belongs next to the benefits, not behind them. A complete case includes a project plan built on your own scope, an estimate of the internal time the project needs, and a view of what the first two closes after go-live will involve. Implementation is one input to a platform decision. For the reasons finance leaders give for choosing Sage Intacct, such as real-time insight, less manual work and audit readiness, read why finance leaders choose Sage Intacct. 

Sage Intacct is cloud accounting and financial management software for mid-sized and growing businesses. The core financials and platform pages describe what it covers, including integration with other solutions, and you can learn more on the Sage Intacct page.

Cloud ERP implementation FAQs 

			

			

	

How long does a cloud ERP implementation take?

	

			

It depends on the number of entities, the number of integrations, data quality, and how much time the finance team can commit. Ask for a plan based on your scope, with its assumptions stated, rather than relying on a typical figure. 

	

	

What is parallel running? 

	

			

Parallel running means operating the old and new systems side by side for at least one full period close and comparing the results. Every difference is investigated and explained before the old system is retired. 

	

	

Who is needed from the finance team? 

	

			

A project sponsor with decision-making authority, a lead who owns design decisions, subject-matter experts for each process area, and champions who support colleagues after launch. These people need protected time, not just goodwill. 

	

	

What are the main risks of a cloud ERP implementation? 

	

			

The most common are poor-quality data being migrated unchanged, integrations that were not fully mapped, too little attention to user adoption, and cutting parallel running short under time pressure. Each is manageable when it is planned for early.

title: AI in Finance: What UK Finance Leaders Need to Know
snippet: AI in finance applies machine learning and automation to anomaly detection, AP automation, forecasting and drafting. This guide covers where it helps, what it needs, the risks and where to start. The post AI in Finance: What UK Finance Leaders Need to Know appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
AI in finance is the use of machine learning and automation to take on work that once needed manual effort or repeated judgement: spotting unusual transactions, processing supplier invoices, building forecasts and drafting commentary. For UK mid-market finance leaders, the practical questions are where to start, what AI needs in order to work, and what has to stay in human hands. 

AI features now appear in many finance tools, and the terminology can blur together. This guide separates the terms, sets out the use cases that suit AI best, explains the prerequisites that determine whether it works, and lists the risks worth managing from the start. It is written for FDs, financial controllers and CFOs who want a clear, balanced picture before committing time or budget.

Key takeaways

Four use cases suit AI well. Anomaly detection, AP automation, forecasting and drafting commentary all involve high volumes or recognisable patterns. 

Data quality is the main prerequisite. AI works on the data it is given, so inconsistent coding and fragmented systems limit what it can do. 

Integration matters as much as the tool. AI that sits outside the finance system creates extra manual steps instead of removing them. 

Human review stays in the loop. AI can flag, draft and suggest, but people remain accountable for decisions and approvals. 

Start with one contained process. A narrow pilot with a baseline and a named owner teaches more than a broad programme. 

Here’s what we cover:

What the main terms mean 

Vendors use “AI” for several different things. Knowing which one is being described makes it easier to judge what a tool can and cannot do. 

Term 

What it means 

Finance example 

Rules-based automation 

Software follows fixed rules written by people. It does exactly what it is told and nothing more. 

Route any invoice above an agreed value to a named approver. 

Machine learning 

Software learns patterns from historical data and uses them to classify, predict or flag. 

Suggest an account code based on how similar invoices were coded before. 

Generative AI 

Software produces text, summaries or answers from a prompt, based on the data and instructions it is given. 

Draft a first version of variance commentary for a person to review. 

AI assistants and agents 

Tools that combine the above to carry out several steps, within the permissions they are given. 

Gather figures, draft a summary and send it for approval. 

Where AI adds genuine value in finance

Four use cases stand out for finance teams because they combine large volumes of data, or large amounts of routine writing, with patterns that software can recognise. The table sets out what AI does in each, what it depends on, and what a person still reviews. 

Use case 

What AI does 

What it depends on 

What a person still reviews 

Anomaly detection 

Flags unusual transactions, duplicate payments or entries that break normal patterns. 

Clean, consistent transaction history. 

Whether a flag is an error, a one-off or a genuine risk. 

AP automation 

Reads supplier invoices, suggests coding and matches them to purchase orders. 

Accurate supplier and purchase order data; connected systems. 

Exceptions, unusual invoices and approval decisions. 

Forecasting 

Finds patterns in historical data to project cash, revenue or costs. 

Reliable history, consistent definitions and connected data sources. 

Assumptions, outliers and what the business knows that the data does not. 

Drafting and summarising 

Produces first drafts of commentary, summaries and answers to questions about reports. 

Accurate underlying figures and clear instructions. 

Every statement, before it goes to a board, lender or auditor. 

Anomaly detection

Finance teams have always looked for the transaction that does not belong, but sampling only catches so much. AI can scan an entire population of entries and flag those that break normal patterns, such as duplicate payments, unusual amounts or postings to unexpected accounts. It speeds up review. It does not replace it: a flagged item still needs someone to decide whether it is an error, a one-off or a risk. Good anomaly detection also depends on disciplined account reconciliation, which gives AI a trusted baseline to compare against. 

AP automation

Accounts payable combines high volumes, repeatable steps, and clear rules, which makes it a natural fit for AI. Tools can read an invoice, suggest coding, match it to a purchase order, and route it for approval, leaving people to handle exceptions. Our guide to what AP automation is explains the mechanics, and accounts payable management best practices cover the process discipline that makes automation effective. Without that discipline, automation simply speeds up an inconsistent process. 

Forecasting

Forecasting benefits from AI’s ability to find patterns across large data sets and to refresh projections as new data arrives. The value rises when forecasts draw on connected sources, such as billing, payroll and pipeline, rather than a single spreadsheet. Forecasts still need human judgement about assumptions, one-off events and information the data does not contain. For the underlying process, see our guide to budgeting and forecasting and the overview of financial planning software. 

Drafting and summarising

Much of a finance team’s week goes on writing: variance commentary, board pack narrative, responses to routine queries. Generative AI can produce a first draft from the figures, which a person then checks, corrects and approves. The saving is in the first draft, not in the sign-off. Because generated text can read as confident when it is wrong, every figure and every explanation needs to be checked against the source before it leaves finance. 

What AI needs in order to work

Most disappointing AI projects share a cause: the prerequisites were not in place. Three matter most. 

Data quality. Consistent charts of accounts, clean supplier and customer records and agreed definitions. AI will not fix poor data, and it can amplify it. 

System integration. AI needs access to the data where it lives. If invoices, purchase orders, bank data and the ledger sit in disconnected tools, the AI sees only part of the picture, and people end up moving data between systems by hand. 

Process clarity and ownership. Someone must own each AI-assisted process, know what good looks like and be accountable for outcomes. 

A quick readiness check can show where to focus before any tool is chosen. 

Readiness question 

Why it matters 

Is transaction data coded consistently across entities and teams? 

Inconsistent coding is a common cause of unreliable AI output. 

Do your core finance systems share data automatically? 

Manual transfers between systems limit what AI can see and add steps. 

Does each process have a named owner? 

Someone must be accountable for results and for reviewing exceptions. 

Do you know today’s baseline for time and error rates? 

Without a baseline, you cannot show whether AI has helped. 

Integration is a feature of the finance platform as well as of the AI tool. Sage’s Sage Intacct platform page describes integration with other solutions and connectivity for AI applications through the Sage Intacct REST API and MCP Server.

What AI does not do

AI does not understand the business the way a finance team does. It can find a pattern, but it cannot know that a spike in costs reflects a planned acquisition, that a supplier is being paid early by agreement or that a forecast assumption is out of date. It does not take accountability for a decision either: that stays with the people who approve payments, sign off numbers and answer to the board. 

It also does not repair a weak process. If approvals are inconsistent or coding rules are unclear, AI will reproduce those weaknesses faster. A sound approach is to fix the process first, then automate it. 

The risks to manage

None of these risks is a reason to avoid AI. Each is a reason to introduce it deliberately. 

Risk 

What it looks like 

Practical response 

Accuracy 

Output that looks confident but is wrong. 

Test on known data first and sample-check results on an ongoing basis. 

Human review 

Suggestions accepted without scrutiny. 

Define which actions need a person’s approval, and who that person is. 

Access controls 

Tools reaching data beyond what a user should see. 

Apply existing role-based permissions and review what data each tool can access. 

Data privacy 

Confidential or personal data shared with a tool without checks. 

Establish where data is stored and how a provider uses it, and involve your data protection lead before use. 

Audit trail 

No record of what AI suggested or did. 

Keep logs of inputs, outputs and approvals so decisions can be traced. 

Involve your auditors and your data protection lead early. Their questions about records, approvals and data handling are easier to answer when the process is designed with them in mind than when it is explained afterwards. 

Where to start

A practical starting point has three steps. First, choose one contained process with reasonably clean data, such as invoice processing or reconciliation, and record how long it takes and how often it goes wrong today. Second, run a time-boxed pilot with a named owner, clear rules on what needs human sign-off and a review at the end. Third, expand only when the results are measurable and the team trusts the output. Useful measures for the pilot include time taken per task, error and exception rates, the volume handled without manual intervention, and how confident the team feels in the results. 

Involve the people who will review the output from the start, including the financial controller and anyone responsible for controls, so that approval rules and the audit trail are designed in rather than added later. 

As routine work moves to software, the finance team’s time shifts towards analysis and advice. That change in role is covered in from scorekeeper to strategist.

A note on Sage and AI

Sage describes Sage Copilot as “the AI assistant built into Sage products”. Read Sage’s guide to Sage Copilot for how Sage describes its approach to AI for finance. To learn more about the finance software itself, visit the Sage Intacct page.

			

	

Where should a finance team start with AI? 

	

			

Start with one contained process that has clean data and clear rules, such as invoice processing or reconciliation. Record a baseline, run a time-boxed pilot with a named owner, and expand when results are measurable. 

	

	

What data does AI in finance need? 

	

			

Consistent, well-structured data: a standard chart of accounts, accurate supplier and customer records, and connected systems so that AI can see the full picture. Poor data limits what AI can do, and it can magnify errors. 

	

	

What are the risks of using AI in finance? 

	

			

The main risks are inaccurate output, decisions made without enough human review, tools reaching data beyond what a user should see, data privacy and gaps in the audit trail. Each can be managed with testing, clear approval rules, existing access controls, early involvement of your data protection lead and logging. 

	

	

What is the difference between AI and automation? 

	

			

Automation follows fixed rules written by people. AI, such as machine learning, learns patterns from data and uses them to classify, predict or flag. Many finance tools combine both, with people reviewing the results.

title: How to Build a Finance Function That Scales
snippet: A scalable finance function handles more transactions, entities, and reporting without more manual effort. This guide explains when to add a controller, CFO or FP&A, and when systems must change. The post How to Build a Finance Function That Scales appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
A scalable finance function is one that absorbs more transactions, entities and reporting demands without a proportionate rise in manual effort. For a growing mid-market business, building one is less about hiring ahead of the curve than about making a handful of well-timed decisions: when to bring in a controller, when to appoint a CFO, when to add FP&A, and when the systems underneath have stopped keeping up. 

Most guidance on building a finance function describes either a company in its first years or a large enterprise with a full finance organisation. Growing mid-market businesses sit between the two: complex enough to need structure, not yet large enough for the textbook model. This guide is for FDs, COOs and CEOs making these calls, and it frames each one as a set of observable signs rather than a fixed rule.

Key takeaways

Scale comes from leverage, not headcount. A function that needs a new hire for every increase in volume has not been built to scale. 

Each role solves a different problem. A controller protects accuracy and control, FP&A looks ahead, and a CFO links finance to strategy and capital. 

Look for signs, not thresholds. Longer closes, hand-built reports and entities added through acquisition are better triggers than any revenue figure. 

Systems can become the constraint before people do. Hiring into a process that is already manual can make the bottleneck bigger. 

A bottleneck is visible from outside finance. When other teams are waiting for numbers, the structure needs attention. 

Here’s what we cover:

What a scalable finance function looks like

Three roles come up in almost every conversation about scaling finance, and they are often confused. The table gives a one-line distinction for each. 

Role 

Focus 

Problem it solves 

Financial controller 

Accuracy, process and control of the numbers. 

Making sure the books are right, closed on time and auditable. 

CFO 

Strategy, capital and the link between finance and the wider business. 

Using the numbers to steer the business, not only report on it. 

FP&A (financial planning and analysis) 

Budgeting, forecasting and performance analysis. 

Looking ahead, so leaders decide with more than last month’s results. 

The right order and timing depend on where the pressure is. The table below links four common stages to the signs that show up, the capacity to add and what it means for systems. 

Stage 

Signs 

Capacity to add 

System implication 

Finance is holding things together 

The FD still produces most reports personally; month-end takes longer each quarter; errors surface late. 

A controller to own the close and controls. 

Move core processes off spreadsheets. 

Finance is accurate but looks backwards 

The close is reliable, but leaders ask questions finance cannot answer quickly; forecasts are built ad hoc. 

FP&A capacity. 

Planning and reporting that draw on one source of data. 

Finance needs to steer the business 

Acquisitions, new markets, lenders or investors; the board expects a forward view. 

CFO-level leadership. 

Consolidation across entities and flexible reporting. 

Finance is the bottleneck 

Other teams wait for numbers; adding people no longer shortens delays. 

Redesign before hiring more. 

Automation and one platform for finance data. 

These stages are not a strict ladder. A business that grows through acquisition may need CFO-level thinking before its close is fully under control, and a business with a steady, single-entity model may add FP&A before a controller. Treat the table as a way of spotting where pressure is building, not as a timetable.

Controller or CFO: which comes first?

For most growing businesses, the controller comes first, because accuracy and control are the foundation everything else rests on. The signs are practical: month-end takes longer each quarter, the FD is still doing the work of a reporting team, reconciliations slip, or audit queries take days to answer. A controller takes ownership of the close, the controls and the team that runs them, which frees the FD to look outward. 

A CFO becomes the priority when the questions change from “are the numbers right?” to “what should we do with them?” Acquisitions, entry into new markets, conversations with lenders or investors, and a board that expects a forward view are all signs. Many businesses promote an existing FD rather than hire externally; the role shift is explored in from scorekeeper to strategist, and anyone newly stepping into the seat can use the new CFO’s first 90 days checklist.

When to add FP&A capacity

FP&A is usually the third addition, but it is the one leaders feel most when it is missing. The signs are that forecasts are rebuilt from scratch each cycle, budget-to-actual conversations focus on explaining numbers rather than changing course, and finance cannot answer a “what if” question without a week of preparation. 

A sensible first remit for FP&A is narrow: a rolling forecast that is refreshed on a regular cycle, a small set of drivers that explain most of the movement in revenue and cost, and a monthly review that leads to decisions rather than explanations. Once that rhythm is established, scenario planning and deeper performance analysis can follow. 

Tools shape how much a planning team can deliver as much as headcount does. Our guide to budgeting and forecasting covers the process, and financial planning software is worth understanding before deciding how much capacity to add: if the planning process is manual, adding headcount scales the manual effort rather than removing it. 

How finance systems need to evolve

Systems can become the constraint before people do. A business that has doubled its transactions, added entities or opened new revenue streams while keeping the same core tools will see the effects in specific places. 

The close. Manual journals, reconciliations and chasing subsidiary data stretch the timetable. See why UK finance teams can’t close faster. 

Consolidation. Combining entities in spreadsheets becomes harder with every entity added. See multi-entity finance: acquire and expand. 

Payables. Invoice volume grows with the business, and manual matching and approval routing grow with it. See accounts payable management best practices. 

Reporting. Each new stakeholder adds another format to rebuild by hand. 

The principle is to automate what scales with volume, standardise what scales with entities, and keep finance data in one place so that reporting draws on a single source.

Avoiding a finance function that becomes the bottleneck

A finance function becomes a bottleneck when its output cannot keep pace with what the business asks of it. It rarely announces itself inside finance. It shows up as sales leaders waiting for margin figures, operations leaders running on last month’s numbers and board packs finished the night before. 

Bottleneck signal 

What it usually points to 

First fix to consider 

The close lengthens every quarter 

Manual journals, reconciliations and data chasing. 

Automate matching and standardise the close timetable. 

Reports are rebuilt by hand each cycle 

Reporting that sits outside the finance system. 

Report directly from finance data, with fixed definitions. 

Leaders ask the same questions repeatedly 

No agreed view of what leaders need to see. 

Define a short set of decision-ready measures. 

New hires do not shorten delays 

A process that scales with effort, not with volume. 

Redesign the process before adding capacity. 

Three habits help. First, review the structure when the business changes, not when finance breaks: an acquisition, a new market or a new funding arrangement should trigger a review of capacity and systems. Second, measure the function by turnaround, such as time to close and time to answer a question, not by hours worked. Third, decide what leaders need to see and build to that: our guide to building a CFO dashboard that drives decisions shows how.

Putting it together

Scaling finance is a sequence of decisions, not a single project. Each stage has signs that show it is time, and each hire works best alongside a matching improvement in how work gets done. Sage Intacct is cloud accounting and financial management software for mid-sized and growing businesses, and its page is a useful place to start if the signs in this guide sound familiar. 

			

	

What is the difference between a controller and a CFO? 

	

			

A controller focuses on the accuracy, process and control of financial reporting: the close, the books and the audit trail. A CFO focuses on strategy, capital and using financial information to steer the business. 

	

	

When should a growing business hire FP&A? 

	

			

When forecasts are rebuilt from scratch each cycle, budget reviews only explain the past, or finance cannot answer “what if” questions quickly. These signs show that the function is reporting well but not looking ahead. 

	

	

When should a business hire a CFO rather than a controller? 

	

			

A controller usually comes first to secure accuracy and control. A CFO becomes the priority when the business needs strategic financial leadership, for example around acquisitions, new markets, lenders, or investors. 

	

	

How do I know if my finance function is a bottleneck? 

	

			

The clearest sign is other teams waiting for finance numbers. Other signs include longer quarterly closes, reports rebuilt by hand, and headcount additions that no longer shorten delays. 

	

	

What should a growing finance team automate first? 

	

			

Start with processes that grow with transaction volume, such as payables, matching and approvals, and recurring tasks such as reconciliations and the close. These free up capacity without needing new hires.
